source: Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer (full text, PMC)
finding: Re-opened full text (gap 2). 87 publications, 145 comparisons. Far transfer is null against treated (active) controls and small against untreated controls. Only nonverbal ability differs reliably by control type.
numbers: Nonverbal ability: treated controls g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13], k=67; untreated g=0.20 [0.11,0.28], k=53; treated vs untreated difference Q(1)=6.09, p=.01. Verbal ability: 0.05 [-0.07,0.17] (k=22) vs 0.03 [-0.09,0.14] (k=16). Word decoding 0.08 / 0.01. Reading comprehension: 0.15 [0.03,0.27] treated (k=19, significant) vs 0.12 untreated. Arithmetic 0.06 / 0.12 [0.01,0.23]. Verbal WM 0.31 treated, 0.42 untreated; visuospatial WM 0.28 / 0.51; criterion (trained) measure 0.80 treated, 1.88 untreated.
quote: there was no convincing evidence of any reliable improvements when working memory training was compared with a treated control condition
limits: Only the nonverbal domain shows a significant treated-vs-untreated gap; the other domains are near zero either way, so the active-control moderator is real for Gf but not general.
agent_relevance: The control-type effect is real in the biggest WM-training meta-analysis, so any scaffold gain must be measured against an active (matched-effort) control, not against nothing.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme (2016) n-back sub-analysis, moderators, follow-up and publication bias (same paper)
finding: The one significant n-back effect on nonverbal ability with treated controls is driven by a few small, one-test studies where the control group fell from pre to post. Remove the worst study and it is negligible. Follow-up at about 5 months shows no far transfer.
numbers: n-back vs treated controls on nonverbal ability g=0.15 (p=.02); after removing Schweizer, Hampshire and Dalgleish 2011, g=0.10. The five largest n-back effects all had under 20 per group and one Gf test; in four of five the control group dropped more than the trained group rose. Adults g=0.10 and low dose (10 h or less) g=0.13 vanish when those studies are excluded. Follow-up (mean 5 months): nonverbal ability treated controls g=-0.05 [-0.21,0.11], k=12; untreated 0.03 [-0.22,0.28], k=7; arithmetic at follow-up falls to g=0.14 once two studies with falling controls are excluded. Authors report no evidential value in treated-control studies after publication-bias analysis.
limits: Moderators coded: age (child/adult/older), dose (10 h split), design, learner status, training type, publication type; some not run when k<4. Main text read this session; supplementary tables not read.
agent_relevance: Explains why the Jaeggi-style positive result persists in small samples: crossover artefacts (control decline) look like transfer. Check that a scaffold gain does not come from a weak baseline arm that got worse.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training (full text, PMC)
finding: Re-opened (gap 2). The WM-training meta-analysis gives far-transfer effects that are small with passive controls and null with active controls. Near transfer to other memory tasks is robust. Effect size is inversely related to design quality.
numbers: WM training far transfer: passive controls g=0.18 (printed CI [-0.09,0.26], k=34); active controls g=0.05 [-0.05,0.15], k=40. Near transfer to other memory tasks 0.44 SD (active) and 0.46 SD (passive). Music for comparison: 0.25 [0.17,0.34], k=64 passive vs 0.03 [-0.07,0.12], k=54 active.
limits: The printed CI [-0.09,0.26] does not centre on 0.18; probably a typo, so do not rely on it. Short report article with rounded values. The same data were re-analysed with robust variance estimation in Sala and Gobet 2020 with similar results.
agent_relevance: Corroborates Melby-Lervag with an independent coding. The moderator is real for Gf in two meta-analyses, though Soveri 2017 finds only a 0.03 difference (K05 stays contested).

source: Sala and Gobet (2020) Working memory training in typically developing children: a multilevel meta-analysis (full text)
finding: Larger multilevel meta-analysis of children. Near transfer scales with task similarity. Far transfer to intelligence, maths and language is essentially zero with active controls, and true heterogeneity is zero once control type and artefacts are modelled.
numbers: m=41 studies, k=393 effect sizes, N=2,375. Far-transfer active-control g=0.001, SE=0.055, p=.982. Nearest-transfer g=0.468 (SE 0.072, 95% CI [0.310,0.626], m=20, k=76); one influential case removed g=0.451. Type of near transfer significant moderator (p=.005); baseline and age not significant (p=.154, p=.914).
limits: Children only. The authors conclude there is no reason to keep investing in WM training with typically developing children, a policy claim beyond the data. Same author group as Sala and Gobet 2017, so not independent labs.
agent_relevance: Post-2017 pooled evidence (gap 6): bigger sample, same answer. Near transfer tracks task overlap, so an agent cannot buy reasoning by practising a memory probe.

source: Gobet and Sala (2022) Cognitive training: a field in search of a phenomenon (full text, PMC)
finding: Second-order meta-analysis of far transfer across ten populations or training types (WM training in four age groups, video games, music, chess, exergames) using data from Sala et al. 2019. Naive pooled effect is small; with active controls only it is zero, with no true heterogeneity.
numbers: Uncorrected far transfer: grand mean g=0.12, true between-meta-analysis variance 0; WM training first-order means 0.13 (TD children, k=25), 0.12 (LD children, k=18), 0.12 (adults, k=44), 0.13 (older adults, k=32). Active controls only: grand mean g=0.00; WM 0.01 (TD children, k=15), 0.02 (LD, k=12), 0.00 (adults, k=27), 0.01 (older adults, k=16).
limits: Position paper by the same authors replying to Green et al. 2019, a consensus statement from the optimistic side; treat the tone as advocacy. Numbers come from their own prior meta-analysis. I did not read Green et al.
agent_relevance: Gives a prior: expect about zero far transfer from any practice stage once the control is active. The same lesson applies to scaffold evaluation (K09).

source: Pahor, Seitz and Jaeggi (2022) Near transfer to an unrelated N-back task mediates the effect of N-back working memory training on matrix reasoning (full text, PMC)
finding: Three RCTs, 460 people, all with no-contact control. The group effect on Matrix Reasoning appears in the retrospective sample and fails in the replication sample. Authors argue far transfer runs only through near transfer to an untrained n-back task.
numbers: Retrospective sample: training effect on post Matrix Reasoning B=0.23 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.43), p=.022, beta=.10, controlling for pre-test. Replication sample: B=0.07 (-0.12 to 0.29), p=.50, beta=.03. Training raised post-test untrained n-back B=1.05, p<.001; n-back to Matrix Reasoning B=0.18 (0.09 to 0.28); indirect effect 0.19 (0.09 to 0.31). Countermanding mediator -0.02 (-0.06 to 0.01). Mediation held in all three RCTs, even RCTs 2 and 3 with no total effect.
limits: Passive (no-contact) control, the design the meta-analyses say inflates Gf effects. Mediation is correlational: people who gain on n-back may be those who gain on matrices anyway. Authors are from the original lab line.
agent_relevance: Best recent pro-transfer evidence and still conditional: the only path is via a near-transfer task with the same structure. For our agent, a gain on an n-back-like probe predicts matrix gains only if the probe shares the mechanism.

source: Blacker, Negoita, Ewen and Courtney (2017) N-back versus complex span working memory training (J Cogn Enhancement; PMC page fetched)
finding: Randomized 3-group study with an active non-WM control (permuted rule operations). Dual n-back and symmetry-span training produced no far transfer to fluid intelligence (BOMAT).
numbers: Experiment 2: 136 enrolled, 73 completed; 20 at-home sessions over 4 weeks. BOMAT: session effect F(1,70)=28.74, p<.001, partial eta2=.29 (all groups improved); group F(2,70)=0.09, p=.91; group x session F(2,70)=0.77, p=.47. Near transfer: dual n-back beat symmetry span (p=.049) and control (p=.002) on an untrained object n-back.
limits: About 20-25 per group, so power for small effects is limited. Single Gf test. WebFetch summary read the first 100,000 of 161,066 characters of the page.
agent_relevance: Another post-2013 active-control failure (gap 6). All groups improving on BOMAT shows practice effects: a scaffold trial needs a matched control to see this.

source: Traut, Guild and Munakata (2021) Why does cognitive training yield inconsistent benefits? A meta-analysis of individual differences in baseline cognitive abilities and training outcomes (full text)
finding: Meta-analysis of the correlation between baseline ability and training gain. Lower baseline went with larger training gain (compensation), but the authors call it inconclusive because heterogeneity is very high and moderators could not be tested.
numbers: Search: 9,502 documents, 555 full-text screened, 42 eligible, 25 papers usable, 82 correlation coefficients. Pooled value printed as 0.4490 (z=4.16, p<.0001); the minus sign was lost in my text extraction, the paper states the correlation is negative. Heterogeneity Q(81)=924.6, I2=91.2%. Egger test z=0.45, p=.65.
limits: All cognitive training, not WM training only, and gain on the trained process, not far transfer. Negative baseline-gain correlations can also arise from regression to the mean (my caveat, not tested in the paper). Too few papers to test domain or strategy-versus-process moderators.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly answered: low-baseline people gain more on trained tasks. This supports per-item scaffold choice (heavy scaffolding where the model is weak, little where it is strong), but only as a trained-task effect, not transfer.

source: von Bastian, Belleville, Udale, et al. (2022) Mechanisms underlying training-induced cognitive change (Nature Reviews Psychology; accepted version)
finding: Review proposing a capacity-versus-efficiency model. Training seldom raises capacity, but often raises efficiency (strategies, routines, better use of the existing limit). Gains on untrained WM tasks follow whether participants can use the learned strategy there.
numbers: Qualitative review. Example: a participant trained on digit span for two years raised span from 7 to 79 items using running-time chunks, with no gain on letter span.
limits: Narrative review; individual-difference moderators come from small studies.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 8: training moves efficiency, not capacity. That matches a scaffold, which changes how a fixed-capacity model uses its context. Transfer needs the new routine to apply in the new task.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) vs Gong et al. (2024), side-by-side reading of prompts and metrics (arXiv 2412.18120 and 2305.03731, PDFs)
finding: Gap 4. I compared the two papers' texts. They differ in prompt format, scoring and models, so the disagreement cannot be pinned on wording alone. I did not run a one-model, equal-token experiment.
numbers: Gong prompt: respond with m whenever the current letter is the same as the letter one, two or three letters ago, and - otherwise; scored by d' with capacity defined as the n where d' falls to about 1; ChatGPT and GPT-4 tested, GPT-4 far above other models. Hu and Lewis: system prompt plus one 24-letter demonstration; the model outputs the retrieved letter and the label; scored by retrieval accuracy and log-probabilities of m-back counterfactual continuations; GPT-3.5, Qwen, Llama and Gemma models. The weakest tier shows a systematic 1-back prior under 2-back instructions.
limits: Different metrics (d' vs retrieval accuracy), model sets and demonstration practice. Nobody has run both prompts on one model at matched tokens. Closed only as a document comparison.
agent_relevance: Do not report one n-back capacity number for an LLM. Fix instruction, demo and metric, and run it on our own model if we want a capacity claim.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: variants incl. reasoning-eliciting instruction (arXiv 2305.03731 PDF)
finding: Gap 5, partial. The think-step-by-step variant (answer first, then the reasoning) did not raise the n-back capacity estimate of ChatGPT: apart from the noise variant, all variants have capacity about 3. No external scratchpad or memory buffer was tested.
numbers: Text: apart from the noise variant, all other variants have a working memory capacity of around 3, d' dropping to around 1 at n=3. Larger spatial grids raised d' (less interference). Open models (Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna-7B and 13B) very low and near-identical; GPT-4 far above others (not tested beyond n=3).
limits: The rationale comes after the answer, so it cannot help the same trial. This differs from Zhang et al. 2024, where step-by-step before the answer lifts WM-bound tasks (K13). Variant d' values were in figures only.
agent_relevance: Written-after reasoning adds nothing. Whether an external buffer helps is a separate question with no direct test found.

source: Pfau, Merrill and Bowman (2024) Let's think dot by dot: hidden computation in transformer language models (PDF)
finding: Gaps 3 and 5, adjacent. Meaningless filler tokens can replace chain of thought and solve hard algorithmic tasks, but only with dense supervision during training. Extra tokens can give compute independent of content.
numbers: Small Llama transformers (34M) reach 100% on 3SUM and 94% on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens and fail without; the filler advantage grows with problem length (up to length 12 for 3SUM). Learning to use filler needs specific dense supervision to converge.
limits: Synthetic tasks, small models trained from scratch, not prompting of frontier models. Earlier work (Lanham et al. 2023) found no filler gains on off-the-shelf LLMs.
agent_relevance: An equal-token placebo is not a clean null: extra tokens can themselves add compute. Use controls with equal tokens of irrelevant text and of content-free filler to separate content from compute.

source: Levy, Jacoby and Goldberg (2024) Same task, more tokens: the impact of input length on the reasoning performance of LLMs (PDF)
finding: Padding with irrelevant text lowers reasoning accuracy at lengths far below the context limit, so an equal-token placebo of irrelevant text can hurt rather than be neutral.
numbers: Average accuracy over tested models falls from 0.92 to 0.68 at about 3,000 input tokens (600 samples per point; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini Pro, Mistral Medium, Mixtral 8x7B). Degradation appears in every dataset version at different intensity; next-word-prediction loss correlates negatively with reasoning performance.
limits: 2023-2024 models; 2026 frontier models may degrade less. Padding is irrelevant text, not a plausible-sounding placebo scaffold.
agent_relevance: Padding controls carry a length penalty. Use two controls, neutral text and a plausible content-free scaffold at equal length, so the scaffold's gain is not overstated.

source: Can (2026) Scaffold, not vocabulary? A controlled, two-tier, pre-registered study of a Popperian code-generation skill (PDF)
finding: Gap 3. A length-matched placebo prompt recovers nearly all of a structured scaffold's gain on a small model, and nothing separates on a ceiling-limited frontier model. The closest LLM analogue of the placebo arm in human training studies.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.6, N=163 HumanEval+: V 95.1%, F 95.7%, L 95.7%, placebo P 96.9%, all pairwise within 2 points, none significant (McNemar). Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, N=164, best-of-8: V@8 34.8%; full skill F@8 and labels-only L@8 both 56.7%; placebo gain +19.5 points; placebo trails F by 2.4 points (paired p=0.60). Same-model 0.5B self-judge 25.6% vs random 24.9-26.8%.
limits: One author, one skill family, code tasks, preprint. Frontier result is ceiling-limited. Best-of-8 sampling confounds scaffold with extra samples. A model has no expectations, so the placebo tests structure and length, not belief.
agent_relevance: Answers the Foroughi-style question in LLM form: a large share of a scaffold's measured gain can be format and length. Our evaluation needs a length-matched placebo and a labels-only arm.

source: Can (2026) Falsification, not exposure: an internally preregistered placebo-controlled decomposition of self-repair feedback in frozen small code models (PDF)
finding: Gap 3. Placebo-mirrored feedback conditions and a matched-budget blind resampling arm. Blind resampling matched real content at pooled level, and some content effect over a generic placebo remained.
numbers: Six benchmark-model cells, three 0.5B-1.5B models, 290 dead task units, 7,000 fresh generations plus 1,400 follow-up. Blind resampling beat bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks (discordant 25/7, Holm p=0.0021). Code-plus-facts beat bare code by +18 (21/3, Holm p=0.00042) and a generic-bullet placebo by +15 (Holm p=0.0041). Instruction-only effect +3, p=0.36. Code-plus-facts and blind resampling both 26 unlocks pooled.
limits: Same single author as d14; 0.5B-1.5B code models; code content stays confounded with prompt length, and the content-attribution result changed direction in a small disjoint sample.
agent_relevance: Compare any scaffold with blind resampling at equal output budget, not only with the plain prompt. A retry arm often explains gains.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to forget: proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs (mitigation section, PDF v3)
finding: Gap 9, partial. Natural-language forget and focus instructions do not help. A mock-QA reset (a simulated earlier query and answer inserted 120 updates before the end) partially helps. Larger models decay more slowly, but the reset was not tested across size tiers or at equal tokens.
numbers: Retrieval accuracy falls log-linearly with update count (3 to 400 updates, 46 keys); L-size models fall more slowly than XS. Per-key forget prompt: under 10 points change at 100 updates, errors clustered at the instruction position. Five interventions tested: per-key forget, forward focus, relevance meta-prompt, soft session reset, mock QA reset. Mock QA reset shown on gemini-2.0-flash, llama-4-maverick, gpt-4.1-mini, mistral-small-2503; described as partial, no single number read from text.
limits: The reset adds tokens and no equal-token control arm was reported. Curves read from figures. Ad hoc prompt with no theory.
agent_relevance: Supports a structured memory reset as a scaffold operation, but the gain must be tested against an equal-token filler turn before crediting the reset content.

source: Xie et al. (2025) Play to generalize: learning to reason through game play (ViGaL), ablations (PDF v4)
finding: Gap 10, partial. Label and training-method controls exist and matter: random labels give no gain, and SFT on identical game data hurts. No ARC test.
numbers: Qwen2.5-VL-7B base average 49.1 (Math 47.7, CLEVR+ 54.9, Geometry 44.8). Snake RL: 62.3 (Math 49.4, CLEVR+ 82.6, Geo 55.0). Random-label RL: 49.4, no gain. SFT on the same Snake data: 47.2 (Math 38.0, Geo 32.1), i.e. -9.7 on math and -12.7 on geometry. Text-only input 59.6 vs vision+text 62.3; reasoning-instruction prompt +1.9; best-and-worst-move reward +1.8; 16K samples 60.1 vs 36K 62.3.
limits: One base model, multimodal math and spatial benchmarks. Averages include CLEVR+, which is close to the game domain. The random-label result differs from text-math RLVR papers; the authors blame base model and data domain. No ARC-AGI evaluation.
agent_relevance: RL with a verifiable reward on a game transfers to math, but SFT on the same data does not: how you practise matters. The human WM-training analogue holds only for goal-checked active practice.

source: Liu et al. (2026, ICLR) SPIRAL: self-play on zero-sum games incentivizes reasoning via multi-agent multi-turn RL (tables, PDF v3)
finding: Gap 10, partial. Self-play RL beats SFT on the same games across 8 reasoning benchmarks, but the gain shrinks for models already tuned for instruction or reasoning. No ARC evaluation in the paper.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base average 34.0; SFT-Kuhn 37.4; SFT-Multi 39.7; SPIRAL-Kuhn 43.4; SPIRAL-Multi 44.5 (+10.5). Qwen3-8B-Base 39.5 to 49.6 (SFT-Multi 46.1). Octothinker-8B-Base 25.8 to 33.8 (SFT 27.0). Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 23.9 to 25.9 (+2.0; SFT 25.0). DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B 60.4 to 61.8 (+1.4; SFT 58.3). Random opponents cause collapse.
limits: Gains are largest on base models; ceilings and prior RL tuning limit the rest. Benchmarks are math and science multiple choice, not matrices. Models abandon reasoning after about 200 steps without the paper's stabiliser.
agent_relevance: A boundary analogue of human baseline and ceiling effects (gaps 7 and 8): the stronger the starting model, the smaller the gain. Why ARC does not benefit (gap 10) stays unanswered.

source: Negative search: LLM fine-tuned on n-back or span tasks then tested on reasoning with equal-compute control (web search, Nov 2026)
finding: Gap 1 stays open. A targeted web search for fine-tuning an LLM on n-back or working-memory tasks with matrix or ARC-style transfer found only probing papers (Hu and Lewis; Gong et al.; Zhang et al.), no training study. The arXiv API returned empty results this session, and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited, so the search was thin.
numbers: 0 training studies found in 1 web search; API searches failed or returned unrelated hits.
limits: Absence from a limited search is not evidence of absence. Nearest analogues are game RL (d17, d18) and RLVR transfer (K17).
agent_relevance: Possible experiment: fine-tune or practise in context on n-back, then test on a held-out matrix set with an equal-token neutral-task control. Not run.

source: Negative search: external memory buffer versus free chain of thought on n-back or tracking at equal tokens (web search, Nov 2026)
finding: Gap 5 stays open. No paper found that compares an external scratchpad or memory tool with the same tokens of free chain of thought on n-back or hidden-state tasks. Huang et al. 2025 only note that external vector databases may mitigate the limits.
numbers: 0 head-to-head studies found in 2 web searches. Closest: Gong 2024 reasoning variant (d11, no gain) and Zhang 2024 (CoT lifts Math Magic from 0-26% to 96.7% with o3-mini; earlier note c09).
limits: Thin search for the same reasons as d19.
agent_relevance: Our own experiment: n-back-like probe with (a) visible explicit state record, (b) same tokens of free reasoning, (c) no reasoning.

source: Search for large multi-site WM-training RCTs after Soveri 2017 (web search plus PMC lookups)
finding: Gap 6. I found no large multi-site randomized trial of n-back or WM training after 2017 that reverses the null. Post-2017 evidence is meta-analyses (d03 to d05) and small to mid RCTs (Blacker 2017, 73 completers; Pahor 2022, 460 across three RCTs, passive control). A 2025 preregistered trial mentioned in search output could not be identified or opened.
numbers: Sala et al. 2019 older-adult meta-analysis: far transfer g=-0.008 with active controls (from search-result text only, not opened). Gobet and Sala 2022 grand mean 0.12 naive, 0.00 active.
limits: Several items appeared only as titles (for example a 2020 PsyArXiv 'Working memory training does not improve executive functioning or fluid intelligence'); not opened.
agent_relevance: No post-2017 evidence changes the conclusion; weight stays on the active-control nulls.
